## Introduction

The Iris dataset [@fisher1936use] contains 150 flower measurements across three
species (*Iris setosa*, *Iris versicolor*, *Iris virginica*), with 50 observations
per species. Four morphological features are measured for each flower: sepal length,
sepal width, petal length, and petal width (all in cm).

This notebook uses `NaiveMFLFRMixDClust` to **cluster these 150 flowers without ever seeing the
species labels** - treating the problem as a purely unsupervised task. We then
compare the discovered clusters against the true species to validate the result.
Along the way, every diagnostic and visualization function in the package is
demonstrated.

::: {.callout-note}
The point is not simply to recover three groups from a famous dataset. The point is
to see what `NaiveMFLFRMixDClust` does automatically: it selects $K$ from scratch, decides
which features actually drive the cluster structure, and produces interpretable
subtype profiles - all from a single function call.
:::

## Setup

```{julia}
using NaiveMFLFRMixDClust
using CSV, DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf
```

## Loading the Data

```{julia}
iris = CSV.read(joinpath(@__DIR__, "../data/iris.csv"), DataFrame)
println("Dimensions: ", size(iris))
first(iris, 5)
```

The four continuous features will be standardized before fitting (zero mean, unit
variance), as expected by Gaussian margins.

```{julia}
feature_names = ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"]

dataset = Vector{Any}(undef, 4)
for (j, col) in enumerate([:sepal_length, :sepal_width, :petal_length, :petal_width])
    v = Float64.(iris[!, col])
    dataset[j] = (v .- mean(v)) ./ std(v)
end

# True species labels (for validation only - never shown to the model)
species_map = Dict("Iris-setosa" => 1, "Iris-versicolor" => 2, "Iris-virginica" => 3)
labels_true = [species_map[s] for s in iris.species]

println("n = ", length(labels_true), ", K_true = ", length(unique(labels_true)))
```

## Fitting the Model

We start with $K_{\text{fit}} = 8$ components (deliberately over-specified) and let
the sparse Dirichlet prior plus post-hoc pruning select the true $K$ automatically.

### SFRM - Shared Feature Relevance Model

Under `SFRM()`, each feature has a single relevance probability shared
across all clusters: a feature is either relevant to the clustering or not,
uniformly across all groups.

```{julia}
Random.seed!(42)
res_sfrm = mixClust(dataset, 8;
                    model_setting = SFRM(),
                    u0       = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 2000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    compact  = true,
                    n_init        = 10,
                    max_iter_init = 10)

K_sfrm = size(res_sfrm.w, 2)
@printf("SFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 2000 iterations)\n",
        K_sfrm, length(res_sfrm.elbo_history))
```

### LFRM - Local Feature Relevance Model

Under `LFRM()`, each feature can be relevant in some clusters but not in
others - allowing finer, subgroup-specific signal.

```{julia}
Random.seed!(42)
res_lfrm = mixClust(dataset, 8;
                    model_setting = LFRM(),
                    u0       = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 2000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    compact  = true,
                    n_init        = 10,
                    max_iter_init = 10)

K_lfrm = size(res_lfrm.w, 2)
@printf("LFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 2000 iterations)\n",
        K_lfrm, length(res_lfrm.elbo_history))
```

## Diagnostics and Visualizations

We now run through all eight visualization functions in the recommended workflow
order, using the SFRM result as the primary example (differences for LFRM are
highlighted where they exist).

### Convergence

```{julia}
plot_elbo(res_sfrm; title = "ELBO Convergence - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_elbo(res_lfrm; title = "ELBO Convergence - LFRM")
```

A monotonically increasing curve reaching a plateau confirms that CAVI converged.

### Cluster Sizes

```{julia}
plot_cluster_sizes(res_sfrm; title = "Cluster Sizes - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_cluster_sizes(res_lfrm; title = "Cluster Sizes - LFRM")
```

With three balanced species of 50 flowers each, we expect roughly equal cluster
sizes. The bar chart immediately shows whether the inferred partition is balanced
or dominated by one large group.

### Assignment Confidence

```{julia}
plot_assignment_confidence(res_sfrm; threshold = 0.9,
                           title = "Assignment Confidence - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_assignment_confidence(res_lfrm; threshold = 0.9,
                           title = "Assignment Confidence - LFRM")
```

A distribution concentrated near 1 means individuals are assigned crisply to a
single cluster. A spread toward $1/K$ signals ambiguity - which is expected for
flowers that lie near a species boundary.

### Feature Relevance - PIP

```{julia}
plot_pips(res_sfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
          title = "Posterior Inclusion Probabilities - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_pips(res_lfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
          title = "Posterior Inclusion Probabilities - LFRM")
```

### Feature Relevance - EIG

```{julia}
eig_sfrm = compute_eig(res_sfrm.margins, res_sfrm.w, res_sfrm.pip)
plot_eig(eig_sfrm, 0.20; feature_names = feature_names,
         title = "Expected Information Gain - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
eig_lfrm = compute_eig(res_lfrm.margins, res_lfrm.w, res_lfrm.pip)
plot_eig(eig_lfrm, 0.20; feature_names = feature_names,
         title = "Expected Information Gain - LFRM")
```

Active features (EIG ≥ 0.20):

```{julia}
active_sfrm = filter_features(eig_sfrm, 0.20)
active_lfrm = filter_features(eig_lfrm, 0.20)
println("SFRM active: ", feature_names[active_sfrm])
println("LFRM active: ", feature_names[active_lfrm])
```

It is well established in the literature that petal measurements are the most
discriminative features for separating Iris species; sepal width is often near-noise.
The EIG ranking should reflect this directly.

### Local PIPs (LFRM)

```{julia}
plot_local_pips(res_lfrm; feature_names = feature_names,
                title = "Per-Cluster Mean PIPs - LFRM")
```

This plot is only meaningful for `LFRM()`. It reveals whether some features
are relevant only in a subset of clusters - a finer picture than the global PIP bar
chart can provide.

### Subtype Feature Profiles

```{julia}
plot_profiles(res_sfrm, dataset; feature_names = feature_names,
              title = "Feature Profiles - SFRM")
```

```{julia}
plot_profiles(res_lfrm, dataset; feature_names = feature_names,
              title = "Feature Profiles - LFRM")
```

Each cell shows the cluster's expected value as a z-score relative to the
population background. Red = above background, blue = below. The three Iris
species have well-known morphological signatures: *setosa* has large sepal width
and short petals, while *virginica* has long petals; these should appear as
distinct rows.

### Cluster Assignments in Feature Space

```{julia}
plot_assignments(res_sfrm, dataset;
                 x_feature = 3, y_feature = 4,
                 feature_names = feature_names,
                 title = "Cluster Assignments - SFRM (petal space)")
```

```{julia}
plot_assignments(res_lfrm, dataset;
                 x_feature = 3, y_feature = 4,
                 feature_names = feature_names,
                 title = "Cluster Assignments - LFRM (petal space)")
```

Petal length and petal width (features 3 and 4) are the most discriminative; the
three species form near-separable groups in this 2D projection.

## External Validation

The species labels were never shown to the model. We now compare the inferred
partition against the true species using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI):
ARI = 1 means a perfect match, ARI = 0 means chance-level agreement.

```{julia}
function compute_ari(labels_true, labels_pred)
    n = length(labels_true)
    classes  = unique(labels_true)
    clusters = unique(labels_pred)
    C, K = length(classes), length(clusters)
    cont = zeros(Int, C, K)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = findfirst(==(labels_true[i]),  classes)
        ki = findfirst(==(labels_pred[i]), clusters)
        cont[ci, ki] += 1
    end
    s_ij = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, cont)
    s_i  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=2))
    s_j  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=1))
    exp  = (s_i * s_j) / (n*(n-1)/2)
    mx   = 0.5*(s_i + s_j)
    mx == exp && return 1.0
    return (s_ij - exp) / (mx - exp)
end

pred_sfrm = res_sfrm.labels
pred_lfrm = res_lfrm.labels

ari_sfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, pred_sfrm)
ari_lfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, pred_lfrm)

@printf("ARI vs true species:  SFRM = %.3f   LFRM = %.3f\n", ari_sfrm, ari_lfrm)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
conf_sfrm = round(mean([maximum(res_sfrm.w[i, :]) for i in 1:150]), digits=3)
conf_lfrm = round(mean([maximum(res_lfrm.w[i, :]) for i in 1:150]), digits=3)

println("Summary")
println("─────────────────────────────────")
@printf("  %-8s  K̂ = %d   ARI = %.3f   confidence = %.3f\n",
        "SFRM", K_sfrm, ari_sfrm, conf_sfrm)
@printf("  %-8s  K̂ = %d   ARI = %.3f   confidence = %.3f\n",
        "LFRM", K_lfrm, ari_lfrm, conf_lfrm)
```

An ARI close to 1 on Iris is a strong sanity check: it confirms that
`mixClust` correctly recovered three groups, selected $K$ automatically from
$K_{\text{fit}} = 8$, and identified petal features as the primary drivers -
consistent with decades of botanical literature on this dataset.

## Out-of-Sample Prediction

```{julia}
# Hold out the last 15 flowers (5 per species) and predict their cluster
test_data  = [dataset[j][136:end] for j in 1:4]
train_data = [dataset[j][1:135]   for j in 1:4]

Random.seed!(42)
res_train = mixClust(train_data, 8;
                     model_setting = SFRM(),
                     u0 = 0.01, max_iter = 2000, tol = 1e-5, compact = true,
                     n_init = 5)

w_test = predict_subtypes(res_train, test_data)

println("Held-out flowers - predicted cluster probabilities (top column = dominant cluster):")
for i in 1:15
    dom = argmax(w_test[i, :])
    @printf("  flower %3d (true: %s)  →  cluster %d  (confidence %.3f)\n",
            135+i, iris.species[135+i], dom, w_test[i, dom])
end
```

## Takeaways

- `mixClust` recovered $K = 3$ automatically from $K_{\text{fit}} = 8$.
- Petal length and petal width were flagged as the most informative features
  by both PIP and EIG - consistent with the known biology of the dataset.
- Sepal width received low EIG, correctly identified as near-noise for separating
  these three species.
- `predict_subtypes` assigns held-out flowers to the learned clusters with high
  confidence, demonstrating the model's generalization to new observations.
